subject: Career
title: Documentation as Communication
description: A micro-lesson that makes Documentation as Communication usable.

hook.text: The answer exists. It's in someone's head. They're on vacation. Now the project is blocked for a week.

buildup.text: Undocumented knowledge is organizational risk. When people leave, so does their knowledge.

discovery.text: Good documentation scales you: it answers questions when you're not available, forever.

twist.text: Most documentation fails because it's written once and never updated. Living docs beat perfect docs.

climax.text: Write docs for your future self who has forgotten everything. If that person can follow it, anyone can.

punchline.text: If it's not documented, it didn't happen — and it won't happen again.

quiz.question: Why is documentation critical in workplace communication?
options: It scales knowledge and prevents project blocks when people are unavailable

details.summary: Documentation is an asynchronous communication medium that enables knowledge transfer across time and teams. Good documentation reduces dependency on individual knowledge holders, speeds onboarding, and creates institutional memory that survives role changes and turnover.
details.whyItMatters: Organizations that document well reduce onboarding time by up to fifty percent. Undocumented knowledge becomes a liability when key team members leave or change roles.
takeaways: Documentation reduces single points of knowledge failure
Write for the reader who will use it six months from now
Keep docs close to the work: in-repo, in-tool, not hidden wikis

faq.question: What should be documented versus left as tribal knowledge?
faq.answer: Document anything that would take more than five minutes to explain to a new team member: processes, decision rationale, architecture choices, and recurring procedures. Leave truly ephemeral information like daily stand-up notes as verbal unless decisions were made.

faq.question: How do I convince a team that resists writing documentation?
faq.answer: Start by documenting something the team struggles with repeatedly, like a deployment process. When it saves time visibly, use that as a case study. Lower the barrier by using templates and keeping documentation lightweight. Make documentation part of the definition of done.
